summary: Satellites have watched Bangladesh burn for over 20 years, but the same fire was counted two to five times — once per satellite, once per pixel. MODIS reports far fewer detections than VIIRS, not because there are fewer fires, but because its 1 km pixels miss the smaller fires VIIRS sees at 375 m. AgniCalendar harmonizes the record: vegetation detections (NASA FIRMS type 0) on the same UTC date whose centres are within 1.0 km become one fire event, regardless of sensor. From 244,308 raw FIRMS detections for Bangladesh (2003–2024) this produces 117,602 harmonized fire events. The peak month is April 2023 with 4,746 events. A monthly climatology (2019–2024) flags critical months above one standard deviation, like January 2019 and June 2023. The result is a public web calendar any responder, scientist or land manager can open with no login.
details: Title: AgniCalendar — One Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar for Bangladesh. Inspiration: satellites have watched Bangladesh burn for over 20 years, but the same fire was counted two to five times, once per satellite, once per pixel, so fire managers had no consistent picture of when burning really peaks. What it does: AgniCalendar harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into one burning activity calendar for Bangladesh — a public web calendar with a year-by-month heatmap, raw-vs-harmonized yearly totals, and a critical-periods list, with the method and limitations stated on the page. No login needed. It also serves the same calendar from a FastAPI backend (GET /v1/harmonized/calendar). How it was built: vegetation detections (NASA FIRMS type 0) on the same UTC date whose centres are within 1.0 km (haversine) are merged into one fire event, regardless of sensor; FRP is never summed across sensors because MODIS and VIIRS pixels differ. Built from 40 NASA FIRMS yearly country files for Bangladesh (MODIS 2003–2024, VIIRS S-NPP 2013–2024, VIIRS NOAA-20 2019–2024). Challenges: the sensors see different fires, FRP is not comparable across pixel sizes, and the 2025–2026 yearly files are not published yet. Accomplishments: 244,308 raw detections became 117,602 harmonized events (2.08 detections per event); the peak month is April 2023 with 4,746 events; 13 critical months flagged, including January 2019 (z +1.94) and June 2023 (z +1.80, unusual for a normally quiet month); March–April is the burning season in all 22 years. What was learned: counting pixels exaggerates burning whenever a new sensor arrives — harmonization matters more than raw counts. What's next: add 2025–2026 when FIRMS publishes them, extend the same method to other countries, and add a near-real-time window via the FIRMS API. Links: code at https://github.com/mdtanzimulislamrefat/AgniCalender_Final ; interactive demo at https://muse.ai/s/agnicalendar-ry6xbxlemxektxx/__IYU-DKJxKAshOTkUyrrIgi_Uc7viwcQuCEkIc-I3s ; method note in the repo at backend/data/output/HARMONIZATION_METHOD.md. AI disclosure: AI tools were used for coding assistance and for drafting this submission text. All numbers in the calendar were computed by the project's own code from real NASA FIRMS files — no figure was hand-entered or generated by AI. No AI-generated images or video are in the demo; the heatmap and charts are drawn from the computed data.
